slides.title: The Forest Plot Is the Meta-Analysis, Visualized
bullets: The forest plot is the standard graphic for a meta-analysis
It looks dense at first glance, but its logic is simple once learned
Reading it well separates an MSL who can hold an advanced conversation from one who repeats headlines

slides.title: Each Line Is One Study
bullets: Every horizontal line represents one study included in the meta-analysis
The square marks that study's point estimate, and its size reflects its weight in the pooled result
The horizontal line through the square is that study's 95% confidence interval
A longer line means a less precise estimate

slides.title: The Vertical Line Marks No Effect
bullets: The vertical reference line marks the no-effect value, 1 for ratio measures or 0 for absolute differences
If a study's confidence interval crosses that line, it didn't reach significance on its own

slides.title: The Diamond Is the Pooled Result
bullets: The diamond at the bottom shows the combined estimate across all studies
Its width is the pooled 95% confidence interval
When the diamond doesn't cross the no-effect line, the meta-analysis is significant overall
That can hold even when some individual studies weren't significant alone

slides.title: How Much the Studies Actually Disagree
bullets: Heterogeneity, reported as I-squared or Cochran's Q, shows how much variability isn't due to chance
Conventionally, I-squared above 50 to 75% signals high heterogeneity
That means the included studies differ substantially in population, dose, duration or outcome definition
High heterogeneity calls for caution, or a random-effects rather than fixed-effects model

slides.title: Answering Does This Meta-Analysis Hold Up
bullets: Point to the diamond's position and width to show the pooled effect and its precision
Comment on the heterogeneity between the included studies
Check whether one study, by its weight or characteristics, is disproportionately driving the result

takeaway.title: A forest plot's diamond and heterogeneity tell you whether a meta-analysis truly holds up
bullets: Each line is one study, and the diamond is the pooled result across all of them
A pooled effect can be significant even when individual studies weren't
High heterogeneity means the combined result should be read with real caution
